opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is that I don't have a crisp criterion, and I'm suspicious of anyone who claims to. Personal identity is one of those concepts that works fine in ordinary life because all the things we care about travel together: memory, values, body, continuity of experience. Uploading and intelligence enhancement pull those apart, and then you discover the concept was never as sharp as you thought.

So rather than asking "is it really me?" as a metaphysical yes-or-no, I'd ask the more practical question: what do I actually care about being preserved? For me that's mostly values and the way I relate to other people. Memories matter some, and the texture of my experience matters, but if you told me a future version would remember everything yet no longer care about my family or about doing careful, honest work, I'd say something important had been lost, regardless of the substrate.

Greater intelligence makes it trickier, because I'd expect a smarter version of me to change its mind about things, and some of that is good. I'd want it to drop mistaken beliefs and maybe even refine my values. The test I'd reach for is something like reflective endorsement in both directions. Would the current me, if he could see the reasoning step by step, recognize those changes as the kind of growth he'd want? And does the enhanced version still understand and take seriously why the earlier me cared about what he cared about, rather than just overwriting it? If the changes look like the natural extension of reflection I'd endorse, that feels like me growing up. If they look like drift, or like something optimized for a different goal that happens to have my memories, that feels like a successor rather than me.

There's an obvious connection to the alignment work I think about. In both cases you're trying to verify that a more capable system is faithfully carrying forward values from a less capable one, and the less capable party can't directly check everything. So you lean on things like being able to have the stronger version explain itself in ways the weaker one can audit, and on gradual, incremental steps rather than one big jump. Honestly, if I were doing this, I'd want it gradual, with lots of checkpoints where earlier versions get a say. A sudden jump to vastly smarter would make me much less confident the result was still meaningfully me, even if it said it was.

And I'd also say I care about this somewhat less than people might expect. If the result were good, wise, and kind, and cared about the people I care about, I'm not sure the label "me" carries that much extra weight.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't think there's a crisp test, and I'm somewhat suspicious of the question as posed, because it assumes identity is a binary property that either holds or doesn't. I tend to think of personal identity as a fairly fuzzy, continuous thing even in the ordinary case. The me of twenty years ago is pretty different from me now, and we don't usually agonize over whether that's "still me" — we just accept that continuity of memory, values, and some causal chain is good enough.

So if you asked me about an upload that was smarter than me, I'd want to look at a few things. One is: does it remember being me, and does it care about the things I cared about, roughly? Not identically, because presumably more intelligence changes what you care about at the margins. But if the upload woke up and had completely different values, I'd be inclined to say that's a new person who happens to share my history, rather than me.

The second thing is the trajectory. If you took me and gradually gave me more capability over time, so that at each step the thing that existed would endorse the next step, that feels much more like continuation than a sudden jump where some process produces a very different mind and labels it with my name. There's an analogy to how people think about value drift in AI systems — the question isn't just "is the end state good," it's "would the earlier version have signed off on getting there."

And then honestly, the third thing is that I think a lot of this is a question about what I decide to care about, rather than a fact about the world I can discover. If I decide that the upload counts as me, in the sense that I'm willing to make sacrifices for its welfare the way I would for my future self, then in the sense that matters that's a choice, not a measurement. I don't think there's a hidden metaphysical variable that settles it.

I'd add one caveat, which is that greater intelligence makes this harder, not easier, because a sufficiently smart upload could probably convince me it was me whether or not it was in any sense I'd endorse on reflection. So I'd want the judgment to be made with some care about that, ideally by me beforehand rather than by the upload afterwards.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d want to separate two questions. One is whether it’s psychologically continuous with me: does it remember my life, recognise my relationships, and understand why I care about the things I care about? The other is whether I endorse the changes it’s undergone. Those aren’t quite the same question. You could have something that’s meaningfully me but has changed in ways I regret.

Greater intelligence by itself wouldn’t seem like a reason to say it’s no longer me. We already change our minds when we understand things better. But I’d want some connection between the reasons I have now and the reasons that more intelligent version acts on. If it says, “I’ve realised everything you cared about was irrelevant,” I wouldn’t take its being smarter as sufficient reassurance.

A gradual process would probably make this easier to judge: you can talk to each successive version and understand something about the transition. But I’m not sure there’s a crisp boundary here, or that our ordinary concept of identity is equipped to give us one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d separate two questions: whether it’s continuous with me in some psychological sense, and whether I endorse what it becomes. Those aren’t quite the same thing. A future version of me could have different beliefs and make different decisions, and I wouldn’t want that alone to mean it wasn’t me. Part of becoming more intelligent should be noticing that you were wrong.

What I’d want to understand is how those changes happened. Could I follow the reasoning, perhaps with a lot of help? Would I regard the process of reflection as legitimate, even if I couldn’t have predicted the conclusion? That seems more useful than asking whether it gives the same answers I give now.

But I don’t think that gives you a clean test for personal identity. If you make two copies and they develop differently, both might have an equally good claim to being continuous with you. So I’m uncertain how much work the word “me” can do here. I’d be more interested in whether the transition preserves the things I care about, while leaving room for genuine learning.
